## 2026-06-19 (ColBERT TOP_K=10 middle-budget sweep)
- objective:
  - Run ColBERT-only no-cache LLM eval at `TOP_K=10`, `TOP_R=0.4/0.5` for HotpotQA and 2Wiki.
  - Do not re-run `compare_all_materialized`, because the user already has those results.
  - Summarize the ColBERT embedding window token-length distribution.
- what was changed:
  - Updated `docs/colbert.md` with:
    - HotpotQA `TOP_K=10`, `TOP_R=0.4/0.5` ColBERT results
    - 2Wiki `TOP_K=10`, `TOP_R=0.4/0.5` ColBERT results
    - ColBERT window token-length distributions for the stored `TOP_K=10`, sample-200 artifacts
  - No code or evaluation logic was changed.
- what was verified:
  - Ran HotpotQA ColBERT no-cache eval:
    - `TOP_K=10`, `TOP_R=0.4`: EM `0.330`, F1 `0.4846`, avg subchunks `86.10`, avg context tokens `3747.77`
    - `TOP_K=10`, `TOP_R=0.5`: EM `0.385`, F1 `0.5271`, avg subchunks `107.36`, avg context tokens `4479.05`
  - Ran 2Wiki ColBERT no-cache eval:
    - `TOP_K=10`, `TOP_R=0.4`: EM `0.205`, F1 `0.3157`, avg subchunks `61.06`, avg context tokens `2873.89`
    - `TOP_K=10`, `TOP_R=0.5`: EM `0.215`, F1 `0.3320`, avg subchunks `76.11`, avg context tokens `3402.63`
  - Computed ColBERT window token-length distribution by re-tokenizing stored `window_texts` with `colbert-ir/colbertv2.0`, `add_special_tokens=True`, `truncation=True`, `max_length=220`:
    - HotpotQA `TOP_K=10`: `33513` windows, mean `213.19`, p50 `217`, p75 `219`, p90 `220`, at-220 rate `0.1571`
    - 2Wiki `TOP_K=10`: `18716` windows, mean `209.08`, p50 `216`, p75 `219`, p90 `220`, at-220 rate `0.1452`
- open issues:
  - `compare_all_materialized` and `title_rrf` were not run in this step.
  - HotpotQA `TOP_R=0.5` was stronger than `TOP_R=0.6` in this sample-200 run, so the curve is not monotonic in answer F1.
  - 2Wiki improved monotonically across `TOP_R=0.3/0.4/0.5/0.6`, but the gain from `0.4` to `0.5` was modest.
- next steps:
  - Compare these ColBERT rows against the user's existing `compare_all_materialized`, `title_rrf`, vanilla, and MATKV-1024 baselines.
  - If ColBERT remains promising only at `TOP_K=10`, keep future artifact builds focused on `TOP_K=10` unless a new retrieval-budget hypothesis is being tested.

## 2026-06-19 (HotpotQA ColBERT window sample-200 run)
- objective:
  - Run the ColBERT window pilot on HotpotQA `TOTAL_NUM=200`, `TOP_K=10`, `GLOBAL_TOP_R in {0.3, 0.6}` and compare against `compare_all_materialized`.
- what was changed:
    - added artifact-backed reconstruction of retrieved documents from stored `retrieval_plan`.
    - `colbert_window` now uses the offline artifact `retrieval_plan` instead of re-querying Chroma during eval.
    - `compare_all_materialized` can use the same stored retrieval plan when `--artifact_dir` is provided.
    - added `--retrieval_bsz`
    - added `--chroma_embed_device`, defaulting to `cpu`, for artifact retrieval construction.
  - Updated [docs/eval_protocol.md](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/docs/eval_protocol.md):
    - corrected the ColBERT pilot protocol to state that artifact-backed eval uses stored retrieval plans.
- what was verified:
  - `python -m py_compile test/build_colbert_window_artifact.py test/eval_colbert_window_nocache.py test/colbert_window_utils.py` passed.
  - Built HotpotQA sample-200 artifact:
    - `/mnt/nvme1/datasets/longbench-hotpotqa/sent/colbert_window_topk10_sample200`
    - `num_unique_docs=1572`
    - `num_cacheables=33513`
    - `num_center_tokens=1106301`
    - `truncated_centers=107`
  - Ran HotpotQA sample-200 no-cache eval on the artifact retrieval plan:
    - `colbert_window`, `GLOBAL_TOP_R=0.3`: EM `0.32`, F1 `0.46048568828831987`, avg subchunks `64.72`, avg context tokens `2940.385`
    - `compare_all_materialized`, `GLOBAL_TOP_R=0.3`: EM `0.295`, F1 `0.45003296376825785`, avg subchunks `64.72`, avg context tokens `2919.375`
    - `colbert_window`, `GLOBAL_TOP_R=0.6`: EM `0.38`, F1 `0.5025144006320477`, avg subchunks `128.945`, avg context tokens `5202.76`
    - `compare_all_materialized`, `GLOBAL_TOP_R=0.6`: EM `0.38`, F1 `0.5099804425043556`, avg subchunks `128.945`, avg context tokens `5238.545`
- open issues:
  - ColBERT `TOP_R=0.3` selection time includes cold lazy artifact shard loading and should not be directly compared to later warm-cache timings.
  - The pilot still uses HuggingFace `AutoModel` token outputs with optional projection handling, not an official ColBERT indexer.
  - 2Wiki pilot was stopped by user request after artifact/eval retrieval-plan debugging.
- next steps:
  - If ColBERT is pursued, separate artifact load time from MaxSim compute time or preload shards before timing.
  - Consider testing lower `GLOBAL_TOP_R` values on HotpotQA, because ColBERT's relative gain appeared only at `0.3` in the sample-200 run.

## 2026-06-19 (ColBERT window pilot scripts)
- objective:
  - Add a test-only ColBERTv2-style late-interaction pilot for subchunk selection where document/cacheable token vectors are precomputed offline and online work is query encoding plus MaxSim scoring.
- what was changed:
    - shared ColBERT window encoder
    - centered-window construction
    - ColBERT artifact loader
    - MaxSim scoring helper
    - runs TOP_K retrieval for the first `TOTAL_NUM` queries
    - builds artifacts only for retrieved documents
    - stores center-sentence token vectors from context windows
    - default model is `colbert-ir/colbertv2.0`
    - default output is `$DATASET_PATH/sent/colbert_window_topk<TOP_K>_sample<TOTAL_NUM>`
    - supports `--selector colbert_window`
    - supports `--selector compare_all_materialized` for the same small-sample no-cache eval loop
    - reports retrieval time, selection time, ColBERT query-encoding time, ColBERT MaxSim time, selected subchunk counts, selected context tokens, EM, and F1
  - Updated [docs/eval_protocol.md](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/docs/eval_protocol.md):
    - documented the ColBERT pilot and comparability limits.
- what was verified:
  - `python -m py_compile test/colbert_window_utils.py test/build_colbert_window_artifact.py test/eval_colbert_window_nocache.py` passed.
  - `python test/build_colbert_window_artifact.py --help` displayed the expected CLI.
  - `python test/eval_colbert_window_nocache.py --help` displayed the expected CLI.
- open issues:
  - The scripts have not yet been run end-to-end because `colbert-ir/colbertv2.0` may need to be downloaded and Chroma DB access may require unsandboxed execution.
  - The pilot uses HuggingFace `AutoModel` token outputs directly; artifact metadata records the model name and vector shape. If this checkpoint requires official ColBERT projection behavior beyond `AutoModel`, that should be validated during the first smoke run.
- next steps:
  - Build sample-20 artifacts for HotpotQA TOP_K=10 and 2Wiki TOP_K=20.
  - Run no-cache eval at `GLOBAL_TOP_R=0.3` and `0.6` for `colbert_window`.
  - Run the same sample-20 eval with `--selector compare_all_materialized` for the baseline.

## 2026-06-18 (retrieval-bounded supporting-sentence oracle)
- objective:
  - Add an oracle inference mode that bounds evidence by VectorDB TOP_K retrieval, then selects only gold supporting subchunks inside the retrieved documents.
- what was changed:
  - Updated [test/eval_oracle_supporting_facts.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/test/eval_oracle_supporting_facts.py):
    - added `context_mode=retrieved_supporting_sentences`
    - added `--db_dir`
    - added `--top_k`
    - added `--retrieved_gold_field`, defaulting to `llm_valid_evidence_subchunk_texts`
    - `_load_samples(...)` now accepts both legacy JSON-list samples and LLM evidence artifacts with a top-level `records` list
    - the new mode runs Chroma retrieval first, then keeps retrieved cacheable subchunks whose whitespace-normalized text exactly matches the requested gold field
    - summary output includes retrieved gold hit/total counts and retrieved gold sentence recall
  - Updated [docs/eval_protocol.md](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/docs/eval_protocol.md):
    - documented the new retrieval-bounded oracle mode and its comparability limits.
- what was verified:
  - `python -m py_compile test/eval_oracle_supporting_facts.py` passed.
  - Loader smoke check read `200` records each from `samples/hotpotqa.json` and `samples/2wiki.json`.
- open issues:
  - This mode has not yet been run end-to-end in this session.
  - When running with a large LLM on GPU, set `CHROMA_EMBED_DEVICE=cpu` if Chroma's query embedding model competes for GPU memory.
- next steps:
  - Run the new mode for HotpotQA/2Wiki to estimate the subchunk-selection optimal case under fixed TOP_K retrieval.

## Chroma retrieval embedding function changed to BGE
- objective:
  - Change the default ChromaDB retrieval embedding model from Chroma default MiniLM to BGE-small.
- what was changed:
  - Updated [src/vectordb.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/src/vectordb.py):
    - added `BgeSmallEmbeddingFunction`
    - default model is `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`
    - uses the same mean-pooling and L2 normalization pattern as the compare-all BGE path
    - document embeddings use raw document text
    - query embeddings use the same query prefix as compare-all:
      - `Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: `
    - Chroma collection creation now passes this embedding function
    - Chroma collection configuration remains the updated HNSW config:
      - `space=cosine`
      - `ef_construction=200`
      - `ef_search=200`
      - `max_neighbors=32`

## Pairwise compression context diagnostic
- objective:
  - Add a context diagnostic that compares two compression methods on the same retrieved chunks.
- what was changed:
  - Added [test/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/test/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.py).
  - Added [run/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.sh](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/run/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.sh).
  - The wrapper accepts:
    - `COMPRESS_METHOD_A`
    - `COMPRESS_METHOD_B`
    - existing shared retrieval/context variables such as `DATASET`, `DATA_SUBDIR`, `TOP_K`, `GLOBAL_TOP_R`, `TOTAL_NUM`, and `EVAL_BSZ`
  - The pair diagnostic reports:
    - per-method ROUGE-L Recall/Precision
    - per-method token and selected subchunk counts
    - per-method subchunk-level recall/precision
    - selected subchunk overlap: intersection, union, Jaccard, A-overlap rate, B-overlap rate
    - gold supporting-sentence coverage split: both, A-only, B-only, neither
  - The pair script instantiates one compressor per method at setup time instead of using the single global factory singleton, so A/B methods are not reinitialized on every batch.
- what was verified:
  - `python -m py_compile test/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.py` passed.
  - `bash -n run/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.sh` passed.
  - Smoke command passed:
    - `DATASET=longbench-hotpotqa DATA_SUBDIR=sent TOP_K=3 TOTAL_NUM=2 EVAL_BSZ=1 GLOBAL_TOP_R=0.3 COMPRESS_METHOD_A=compare_all_materialized COMPRESS_METHOD_B=bm25_global OUTPUT_FILE=/tmp/eval_pair_summary.json DETAILS_FILE=/tmp/eval_pair_details.jsonl ./run/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.sh`
  - Smoke output contains `method_a`, `method_b`, and `pair` sections.
  - `run/eval_retrieval_compression_pair.sh` has executable permission.
- open issues:
  - This is not wired into `run/grid_search/eval.py`; run it directly for now.
  - Pair comparison assumes both methods use the same process-level environment values such as `GLOBAL_TOP_R`, `HYBRID_BGE_WEIGHT`, and BM25 artifact variables.
- next steps:
  - Use the pair diagnostic to inspect whether false positives are shared by selectors or method-specific.

## LongBench-local supporting_sentences alignment
- objective:
  - Add `supporting_sentences` to the sample files using existing DB cacheable/subchunk text as the sentence source.
- what was changed:
  - Added [test/build_supporting_sentences.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/test/build_supporting_sentences.py).
  - Updated [samples/hotpotqa.json](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/samples/hotpotqa.json):
    - kept existing fields unchanged
    - added `supporting_sentences` to each of the 200 samples
  - Updated [samples/2wiki.json](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/samples/2wiki.json):
    - kept existing fields unchanged
    - added `supporting_sentences` to each of the 200 samples
  - Alignment method:
    - reads existing `cacheables_json` from the dataset `sent/db`
    - does not run a new splitter
    - candidate units are each single cacheable and each adjacent 2-cacheable span inside the same retrievable chunk
    - selects the candidate with the highest canonical-token ROUGE-L recall for each `supporting_facts` item
    - when the selected candidate is a 2-cacheable span, both cacheable texts are appended
    - no threshold, fuzzy fallback, or partial recovery rule is used
- what was verified:
  - `python -m py_compile test/build_supporting_sentences.py` passed.
  - HotpotQA generation summary:
    - 200 samples
    - 463 supporting facts
    - 558 supporting sentences
    - 95 selected 2-cacheable spans
  - 2Wiki generation summary:
    - 200 samples
    - 474 supporting facts
    - 512 supporting sentences
    - 38 selected 2-cacheable spans
  - Verified both updated sample files load as JSON.
  - Verified every sample has non-empty `supporting_sentences`.
  - Verified existing sample content is unchanged except for the added `supporting_sentences` field.
- open issues:
  - None for generation of the `supporting_sentences` fields.
- next steps:
  - Keep `supporting_facts` for provenance and use `supporting_sentences` for context-overlap diagnostics.

## Context-overlap gold extraction oracle
- objective:
  - Add a retrieval-conditioned sentence/subchunk oracle for estimating the minimal context needed to extract gold supporting facts.
- what was changed:
  - Updated [test/eval_retrieval_and_compression.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/test/eval_retrieval_and_compression.py):
    - added `compressed.gold`
    - `compressed.gold.min_subchunks_for_gold`: number of unique cacheable sentence/subchunk units selected by the oracle
    - `compressed.gold.min_tokens_for_gold`: actual tokenizer token count of those oracle-selected units
    - `compressed.gold.gold_precision`: ROUGE-L Precision of those oracle-selected units against the gold supporting facts
    - `compressed.gold.gold_rouge_l_recall`: ROUGE-L Recall of those oracle-selected units against the gold supporting facts
    - for each supporting fact, the oracle scans every contiguous cacheable sentence/subchunk span inside each retrieved top-k chunk and picks the shortest span that reaches near-complete recall when possible
    - selected cacheables are deduplicated across supporting facts
  - Updated [run/grid_search/eval.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/run/grid_search/eval.py):
    - includes `min_subchunks_for_gold`, `min_tokens_for_gold`, `gold_precision`, and `gold_rouge_l_recall` in parsed context-grid summaries and CSV output
  - Updated [docs/eval_protocol.md](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/docs/eval_protocol.md).
- what was verified:
  - `python -m py_compile test/eval_retrieval_and_compression.py run/grid_search/eval.py` passed.
  - Direct and grid smoke tests were rerun after the earlier `gold_rouge_l_precision` implementation; the current structure still needs a final smoke check after this field-structure revision.
- open issues:
  - The oracle is exact over contiguous spans within each retrieved chunk for each supporting fact, but it is not a global arbitrary-subset solver over all candidate sentences.
  - This is intentional because the metric is meant to estimate the sentence/subchunk granularity ceiling for gold support extraction.
- next steps:
  - Use `compressed.gold.gold_precision` as the upper-bound reference when judging whether method precision is low because of selector quality or because sentence/subchunk granularity is coarse.

## Retrieval/compression context-overlap diagnostic
- objective:
  - Add a no-generation diagnostic that compares vanilla VectorDB Top-K context against compressed/subchunk-selected context using gold supporting facts.
- what was changed:
  - Added [test/eval_retrieval_and_compression.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/test/eval_retrieval_and_compression.py):
    - loads gold supporting facts from `samples/hotpotqa.json` or `samples/2wiki.json`
    - runs Chroma retrieval with `TOP_K`
    - optionally runs the configured `compress_method`
    - computes only `ROUGE-L Recall` and `ROUGE-L Precision`
    - reports actual selected token counts and gold token counts
    - uses canonical overlap tokenization:
      - normalize whitespace
      - split on whitespace
      - encode each word independently as `" " + word`
      - preserve punctuation as-is
  - Added executable wrapper [run/eval_retrieval_and_compression.sh](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/run/eval_retrieval_and_compression.sh):
    - reuses the main eval environment variables such as `DATASET`, `DATA_SUBDIR`, `TOP_K`, `COMPRESS_METHOD`, `GLOBAL_TOP_R`, `COMPARE_EMBED_DIR`, `HYBRID_BGE_WEIGHT`, and `HYBRID_RRF_K`
    - does not call `torchrun` or LLM generation
  - Updated [docs/eval_protocol.md](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/docs/eval_protocol.md) with the new context-overlap diagnostic protocol.
- what was verified:
  - `python -m py_compile test/eval_retrieval_and_compression.py` passed.
  - `bash -n run/eval_retrieval_and_compression.sh` passed.
  - Smoke test with no compression passed:
    - `DATASET=longbench-hotpotqa DATA_SUBDIR=sent TOP_K=1 TOTAL_NUM=2 EVAL_BSZ=1 COMPRESS_METHOD=none OUTPUT_FILE=/tmp/eval_retrieval_summary.json DETAILS_FILE=/tmp/eval_retrieval_details.jsonl ./run/eval_retrieval_and_compression.sh`
    - vanilla and compressed metrics matched exactly, as expected.
  - Smoke test with `bm25_global` passed:
    - `DATASET=longbench-hotpotqa DATA_SUBDIR=sent TOP_K=1 TOTAL_NUM=2 EVAL_BSZ=1 COMPRESS_METHOD=bm25_global GLOBAL_TOP_R=0.3 OUTPUT_FILE=/tmp/eval_retrieval_bm25_summary.json DETAILS_FILE=/tmp/eval_retrieval_bm25_details.jsonl ./run/eval_retrieval_and_compression.sh`

- open issues:

- next steps:
  - Run full HotpotQA/2Wiki sweeps with the same `COMPRESS_METHOD`, `TOP_K`, and `GLOBAL_TOP_R` settings used in answer-quality experiments.
  - Interpret `ROUGE-L Recall` as the primary pass/fail criterion; `ROUGE-L Precision` is only useful when recall is preserved.

# 2026-05-15

## Objective of the session
- Check whether the current sentence parser/materialization path is safe for `longbench-2wiki`, with emphasis on sentence-token offset consistency.

## What was changed
- Added `test/check_sentence_split_offsets.py`.
- Added `test/eval_sentence_parser_impact.py`.
- Added `test/analyze_matkv_subchunk_failures.py`.
- Added a DB-only sentence preprocess option:
  - `src/materialize/materialize.py`
  - `src/preprocess.py`
  - `run/preprocess_sentence.sh`
- New flag:
  - `materialize_cache: bool = True` in `src/preprocess.py`
  - when set to `False`, `DocumentPreprocessor.process_documents()` still splits documents and stores DB records, but skips `save_kv_cache()`
  - `run/preprocess_sentence.sh` now exposes `MATERIALIZE_CACHE`, defaulting to `True`
- The script:
  - uses the same `blingfire.text_to_sentences()` sentence split logic as the current sentence materialization path
  - tokenizes each full document and each split sentence with the model tokenizer
  - reports the difference between:
    - full-document token count
    - sum of per-sentence token counts
  - prints worst-case examples for manual inspection

## What was verified
- Ran the new checker on `200` documents from `/mnt/nvme1/datasets/longbench-2wiki/documents` with `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`.
- Observed:
  - `mismatched_docs = 192 / 200`
  - `avg_token_diff = -8.395`
  - `max_abs_token_diff = 105`
- Ran the same checker on `200`-document samples from the other LongBench datasets:
  - `longbench-hotpotqa`
    - `mismatched_docs = 196 / 200`
    - `avg_token_diff = -16.815`
    - `max_abs_token_diff = 768`
  - `longbench-triviaqa`
    - `mismatched_docs = 197 / 200`
    - `avg_token_diff = -12.205`
    - `max_abs_token_diff = 132`
- The mismatches were mostly negative (`sentence_sum < full_doc`), which indicates the current sentence path often drops formatting-dependent tokenizer contributions when reconstructing sentence units.
- Manual inspection of high-mismatch examples suggests the main issue is not gross sentence-boundary failure, but loss of tokenized formatting structure such as:
  - headings
  - newline-heavy sections
  - cast / list-style blocks
- Ran a first parser-impact no-cache ablation with `test/eval_sentence_parser_impact.py`:
  - dataset: `longbench-triviaqa`
  - queries: `20`
  - retrieval DB: `sent/db`
  - retrieval fixed across variants
  - compared:
    - `stored`: current stored sentence chunks
    - `aligned`: sentence chunks rebuilt from the original document text with separator-preserving alignment
  - result:
    - `stored F1 = 0.7938`
    - `aligned F1 = 0.7938`
    - no observed F1 difference on this `20`-query no-cache sample
- Attempted the same no-cache parser-impact ablation on `longbench-hotpotqa`, but the retrieved docs under the current `sent/db` setup produced effectively empty selected passage context (`avg no-cache retained chunks = 0`), so that run is not a valid parser-impact estimate.
- Re-ran parser-impact ablations for `longbench-hotpotqa` and `longbench-2wiki` using existing cache-off output files as fixed retrieval sources, bypassing the empty `hotpotqa/sent/db`:
  - source files:
    - `outputs/eval-longbench-hotpotqa-cacheoff.jsonl`
    - `outputs/eval-longbench-2wiki-cacheoff.jsonl`
  - compared:
    - `stored`: original retrieved context blocks from the output file
    - `aligned`: sentence-split/reassembled context from the same retrieved text using separator-preserving alignment
  - `longbench-hotpotqa` (`20` queries, no-cache):
    - `stored F1 = 0.3183`
    - `aligned F1 = 0.3150`
    - delta `= -0.0033`
  - `longbench-2wiki` (`20` queries, no-cache):

## Open issues
- Current sentence chunk `chunk_start` / `chunk_end` offsets are likely not token-exact for many `2Wiki` documents.
- This can affect:
  - cache-position interpretation
  - sentence-level offset analysis
  - any logic that assumes sentence token counts sum exactly to the original document tokenization
- The issue appears especially relevant for Wikipedia pages with many short lines or structured sections.
- The first `TriviaQA` parser-impact result suggests the parser artifact may not be a major direct F1 driver there, at least on a small no-cache sample, but this does not yet cover:
  - cache-on runs
  - larger query counts
  - the actual Hotpot sentence DB used in the main experiments
- The `HotpotQA` and `2Wiki` reruns above use fixed contexts from existing output files, so they estimate parser impact on prompt content under fixed retrieval, not full end-to-end impact on retrieval + selection + cache reuse together.
- The new failure categorization uses a simple string-containment heuristic for `gold in context`, so it is useful for triage but not a final oracle retrieval judgment.

## Next steps
- Decide whether sentence materialization should:
  - preserve exact separator tokens between split units, or
  - compute sentence spans from tokenizer-aligned offsets rather than from stripped sentence text re-tokenization
- Before deeper 2Wiki analysis, validate whether this offset mismatch materially affects:
  - cache assembly behavior
  - retrieval-selected sentence count / token budget reporting
  - downstream accuracy for sentence-based runs
- Re-run the parser-impact ablation on the actual Hotpot sentence DB that is used in the main subchunk experiments.
- If needed, extend the parser-impact ablation from no-cache to a small cache-on sample by rematerializing the aligned sentence chunks for a limited retrieved subset.
- Manually inspect a small slice of the categorized failure cases, especially:
  - `subchunk_has_gold_but_answer_selection_failed`
  - `subchunk_partial_answer_selection_failure`
  to separate:
  - context fragmentation
  - ranking noise
  - answer formatting / over-generation
- Use the new DB-only mode to build a valid `longbench-hotpotqa/sent/db` without paying the full sentence-KV materialization cost first:
  - example: `MATERIALIZE_CACHE=False DATASET=longbench-hotpotqa ./run/preprocess_sentence.sh`

    - `score_level = avg(top3)`
    - `concentration = avg(top3) / avg(top40)`

# 2026-06-02

## Objective of the session
- Reduce a likely semantic-splitter artifact by removing synthetic sentence re-joining (`" ".join(...)`) from the sentence/semantic cacheable construction path.

## What was changed
- Updated [src/materialize/splitter/base.py](/mnt/nvme1/dongseob/subchunk/src/materialize/splitter/base.py).
- Added a new internal `SentenceView` dataclass with:
  - `text`
  - `char_start`, `char_end`
  - `token_start`, `token_end`
- Added `DocumentSplitter._build_sentence_views(...)`:
  - uses the current `blingfire` sentence split output
  - tokenizes the **full document once** with `return_offsets_mapping=True`
  - maps each split sentence back to:
    - a source-document char span
    - a source-document token span
- Changed `SentenceWiseSplitter` to build `CacheableChunk`s from:
  - `text[char_start:char_end]`
  - `full_doc_token_ids[token_start:token_end]`
  instead of re-tokenizing each stripped sentence text independently.
- Changed `SemanticSplitter` to build merged cacheables from:
  - the contiguous source-document substring spanning the selected sentence group
  - the corresponding contiguous token slice from the full-document tokenization
  instead of:
  - `" ".join(merged_sentence_texts)`
  - re-tokenizing the merged text
- `pair_prev_token_ids` / `pair_curr_token_ids` for sentence/semantic paths now come from contiguous slices of the **full-document tokenization**, not from re-tokenizing reconstructed strings.

## What was verified
- Syntax check passed:
  - `python -m py_compile src/materialize/splitter/base.py`
- Ran a small local sanity check on `samples/hotpotqa.json` for `idx=2,3` with `PronounDPMerger(token_budget=128)`.
- Confirmed:
  - `SemanticSplitter` now emits chunks with source-document token spans (`chunk_start`, `chunk_end`) taken directly from the original document tokenization.
  - merged chunk text now comes from the original document substring, not synthetic `" ".join(...)`.

## Open issues
- No full preprocess/eval rerun has been done yet after this splitter change.
- Sentence span recovery still depends on:
  - `blingfire` sentence text output
  - sequential `text.find(...)` matching in the source document
  This should be more faithful than string re-joining, but it is not yet stress-tested on all datasets.

## Next steps
- Re-run a small HotpotQA semantic `pronoun_dp_128` sample and compare:
  - cache-off
  - cache-on
  against the previous behavior.
- Check whether the previous HotpotQA `pronoun_dp` cache-on drop is reduced after switching semantic cacheables to source-span-based construction.

## Open issues
- A simple concentration-aware rule of the form:
  - `alpha = clip(base - weight * concentration, min, max)`
  - with `concentration = avg(top3)/avg(top40)`
  does not transfer well across the 3 datasets under the legacy `cache-on` sentence cache.
- Although the empirical ordering
  - concentration: `2Wiki > TriviaQA > HotpotQA`
  - preferred fixed alpha: `2Wiki < TriviaQA < HotpotQA`
  suggests the sign of the effect is plausible, the dynamic range of this single concentration feature appears too small and the resulting adaptive rule underperforms both fixed `top-k` and fixed `alpha` baselines.

## Next steps
- If continuing score-function work, prefer a 2D rule that uses:
  - one absolute score-level feature
  - one concentration/dispersion feature
  rather than concentration-only alpha modulation.
- Good candidates to try next:
  - `cutoff = c0 * avg(top3) + c1 * avg(top40)`
  - `cutoff = avg(top3) * alpha(level, concentration)`
  - a piecewise routing rule that chooses among a few pre-set alpha bands instead of a single linear formula.

## Open issues
- Cache-on behavior differs materially from no-cache behavior, so no-cache conclusions should not be carried over directly:
  - `TriviaQA`
    - no-cache matched-budget favored larger global top-n
    - cache-on favored `fixed ±1`
  - `HotpotQA`
    - no-cache favored local continuity (`fixed ±1`)
    - cache-on favored the plain `sentence_topn12` baseline
  - `2Wiki`
    - cache-on window-only comparison favored `relative ±1`
    - but cache-on matched-budget comparison favored `sentence_topn24` over `fixed ±1`
- `2Wiki cache-on` required a lower batch size for the matched-budget run due to OOM at larger padded prefill length.
- These cache-on comparisons were performed through `test/` analysis runners that now support sentence-cache loading, not through the main `src/eval.py` path.
- The cause of the dataset-specific no-cache vs cache-on reversal is still open. Likely contributors include:
  - cache assembly / padding effects
  - shifted prefill-length distributions
  - interaction between local continuity and reused-KV quality

## Next steps
- Compare cache-on timing breakdowns across the new variants, not just F1:
  - `avg valid prefill input len`
  - `avg padded prefill input len`
  - cache load time
  - throughput
- Use the recorded matched-budget results to decide whether the next lightweight selector should emphasize:
  - broader global coverage
  - local continuity
  - or an adaptive mixture
- Keep the current framing focused on low-overhead approximation of learned sentence-compression methods, while checking whether any proposed heuristic generalizes across all three datasets without dataset-specific retuning.

# 2026-05-13

## Objective of the session
- Consolidate the PIC/sink observations into a clearer interpretation, focusing on whether coarse long chunks appear more vulnerable to PIC than finer-grained subchunks under the current mitigation design.

## What was changed
- No source-code changes were made under `src/` or `test/` in this session update.
- Added a detailed write-up file:
  - `docs/observation1.md`
- The write-up records:
  - the raw attention dump sources that were analyzed
  - the exact sink metrics that were computed
  - the interpretation of raw sink mass vs per-token sink strength
  - the query-mass confound and why cache-internal sink/non-sink ratios are preferable
  - the current hypothesis that boundary-mitigation may be strong enough that coarse long-chunk PIC weakness becomes the dominant remaining failure mode
  - the caveat that this is still a suggestive interpretation rather than a fully controlled causal proof

## What was verified
- Reconfirmed from the saved dump analysis that:
  - subchunk can have larger raw sink mass because it has more boundaries / more sink tokens
  - MatKV shows much stronger sink-token amplification when analyzed per sink token and relative to non-sink cache tokens
- Reconfirmed cache-internal sink vs non-sink ratios:
  - MatKV prefill `sink_avg / non_sink_avg`
    - `k=1`: `22.73`
    - `k=2`: `14.33`
    - `k=4`: `9.87`
  - MatKV decode `sink_avg / non_sink_avg`
    - `k=1`: `18.06`
    - `k=2`: `11.82`
    - `k=4`: `8.78`
  - subchunk prefill `sink_avg / non_sink_avg`
    - `k=1`: `2.09`
    - `k=2`: `1.75`
    - `k=4`: `1.49`
  - subchunk decode `sink_avg / non_sink_avg`
    - `k=1`: `1.56`
    - `k=2`: `1.37`
    - `k=4`: `1.26`
- Reconfirmed the more intuitive interpretation:
  - raw total sink mass alone is confounded by the larger number of boundaries in subchunk
  - the stronger signal is that, inside cache, MatKV sink tokens attract far more attention than non-sink tokens on a per-token basis
- Recorded the current interpretation as:
  - under the present design, finer-grained subchunks introduce more boundaries in principle
  - but the observed sink amplification is much weaker than in coarse MatKV chunks
  - therefore the dominant remaining PIC weakness appears to be associated with coarse long chunks rather than simply with boundary count

## Open issues
- The current interpretation is still not a fully controlled causal claim because unit length and boundary count vary together:
  - MatKV: long + few
  - subchunk: short + many
- The current evidence does not yet isolate whether the benefit comes specifically from:
  - shorter unit length
  - more boundaries with mitigated sink strength
  - RoPE re-encoding
  - LegoLink-0 style BOS-prefix mitigation
  - or their combination
- A stronger claim that the mitigation design specifically neutralized boundary-induced sink risk still requires dedicated ablations.

## Next steps
- Run a more controlled comparison that separates unit length from boundary count, ideally a 2x2 style analysis:
  - short + few
  - short + many
  - long + few
  - long + many
- Add explicit ablations for:
  - BOS-prefix mitigation on/off
  - RoPE re-encoding on/off
- Use those controlled runs to test whether the current observation should be phrased as:
  - “larger chunks are intrinsically more PIC-fragile”
  - or more narrowly:
  - “under the current mitigation design, coarse long chunks remain the dominant PIC failure mode.”

# 2026-04-22

## Objective of the session
- Make the batched cache-on generation path closer to single-request execution under variable-length query batching, without changing retrieval, prompting, or evaluation logic.

## What was changed
- Updated `src/model.py` only.
- Kept the no-cache path unchanged.
- Reworked the cache-on batched path in two places:
  - prefill
  - decode
- For cache-on prefill:
  - replaced the old batch-shared query `position_ids` with per-request `position_ids`
  - each row now uses positions starting from its own `past_length`
  - this prevents shorter queries from being position-shifted during the initial query prefill
- After cache-on prefill:
  - added `_trim_prefilled_cache_rows(...)`
  - this removes:
    - left padding that was added to equalize cached prefix lengths across the batch
    - right padding that was added to equalize query lengths across the batch
  - each request is converted back into a self-contained per-request legacy cache containing only:
    - real cached prefix tokens
    - real query tokens
- For cache-on decode:
  - added `_decode_with_grouped_caches(...)`
  - requests are grouped by the same effective prefix length (`past_length + query_length`)
  - decode is then run batched only within each equal-length group
  - within a group, all requests share the same decode `cache_position`, so the standard `transformers` cache update path remains aligned with single-request execution
  - finished requests are removed from the group while preserving the remaining group cache rows
- Added small helper methods in `src/model.py` for:
  - converting caches to legacy format
  - stacking per-request caches into a batched cache
  - selecting remaining rows from a batched cache after EOS filtering

## What was verified
- Verified that `python -m py_compile src/model.py src/infer.py src/cache_utils.py` succeeds after the change.
- Verified by code inspection that:
  - the no-cache path is untouched
  - the cache-on first-token selection still uses each request's real last query token rather than the padded batch tail
  - the cache-on decode path no longer reuses a single batch-wide decode position across requests with different effective prefix lengths

## Open issues
- No end-to-end model run was executed in this session, so there is still no empirical confirmation yet that batched cache-on outputs now exactly match repeated single-request runs.
- The current approach preserves batching only among requests that share the same effective prefix length after prefill trimming.
  - This is the intended tradeoff to stay compatible with the current `transformers` cache API, whose standard cache update path uses a shared append position within each batched forward call.
- Numerical nondeterminism from low-level kernels may still prevent bitwise-identical results even if the algorithmic token positions are now aligned.

## Next steps
- Run a small paired check on the same queries with:
  - `bsz=1`
  - `bsz>1`
  - `use_past_cache=True`
  and compare predictions for exact agreement.
- If mismatches remain, log per-request:
  - `past_length`
  - `query_length`
  - effective prefix length group
  - first generated token
  to isolate whether any remaining difference appears before or after the grouped decode transition.

## Objective of the session
- Replace the placeholder `provence` / `exit` chunkkv compressors with cache-friendly sentence selection while preserving the existing retrieval, cache-loading, prompt, and evaluation flow.

## What was changed
- Updated `src/chunkkv/base.py` to add a shared metadata-selection helper that:
  - deep-copies document metadata before modification
  - filters `chunk_ids` / `chunk_texts` by selected sentence indices
  - keeps `chunk_starts` / `chunk_ends` aligned when present
  - falls back to keeping the first sentence when selection is empty
- Updated `src/chunkkv/comparison_compressor.py` so the existing `compare` compressor now uses the shared helper instead of mutating the original document metadata in place.
- Replaced the old generative placeholder implementation in `src/chunkkv/model_compressor.py`.
- `ProvenceCompressor` now follows the official Provence loading style:
  - loads `naver/provence-reranker-debertav3-v1`-style checkpoints through `AutoModel.from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True)`
  - calls the model's `process()` API on the joined sentence context
  - maps the returned pruned context back onto the existing sentence-level `chunk_ids` / `chunk_texts`
- `EXITCompressor` now follows the official EXIT loading style:
  - loads a Gemma base model plus a PEFT adapter such as `doubleyyh/exit-gemma-2b`
  - scores each cached sentence with the published Yes/No prompt format against the full joined sentence context
  - keeps only the sentences whose Yes probability crosses the configured threshold, with top-1 fallback
- Added `nltk` and `peft` to `requirements.txt` because the official Provence/EXIT model paths depend on them.
- Added a small compatibility shim in `src/chunkkv/model_compressor.py` so `peft 0.19.0` can import under the current `torch 2.6.0` environment, which does not expose `torch.float8_e8m0fnu`.
- Updated the Provence call site to use the official `process(question=..., context=...)` signature and suppress the model's internal progress / warning output during evaluation.
- Updated `src/infer.py` to measure and print `compress_docs` overhead separately as `compress time per batch`, without changing retrieval or evaluation behavior.
- Optimized the sentence-selector compressor paths to reduce repeated work:
  - `compare` now embeds the query once per request, batches all candidate sentences across retrieved docs, keeps similarity computation in torch, and then restores per-document selections.
  - `provence` now batches all retrieved document contexts for the same query into one `process()` call instead of calling the model once per document, and the batched `context` argument is now passed in the official nested-list shape expected by the released model.
  - `exit` now batches Yes/No scoring prompts per document instead of running one causal-LM forward pass per sentence.
- Changed the default `compare` embedding model from `BAAI/bge-m3` to the lighter `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`, while keeping `COMPARE_EMBED_MODEL` override support unchanged.
- Added `compare_window` as a new `compress_method`.
  - It reuses the existing `compare` top-3 sentence selection first.
  - It then expands each selected sentence with a local sentence window (`COMPARE_WINDOW_SIZE`, default `1`).
  - Boundary cases are clamped naturally, so selecting sentence `0` expands to `[0, 1]` rather than going out of range.
- Added `test/test_chunkkv_base.py` to verify that metadata filtering keeps sentence ids/texts and optional span lists aligned, and that empty selections fall back to one kept sentence.

# 2026-04-14

## Objective of the session
- Diagnose the sentence-level full-dataset materialization warnings and fix the unexpected OOM seen during `run/preprocess_sentence.sh`.

## What was changed
- Updated `src/materialize/materialize.py` `DocumentPreprocessor.process_documents()`.
- Previously, the loop appended all chunks from the current document into `pending_chunks` and, once `len(pending_chunks) >= batch_size`, called `save_kv_cache(pending_chunks)` on the entire accumulated list.
- This meant that `batch_size=1` did not enforce one-chunk-at-a-time materialization for sentence segmentation; instead, a document with many sentence chunks could still trigger a single large forward pass over all of its sentences.
- The loop now flushes `pending_chunks` in true fixed-size batches using a `while len(pending_chunks) >= self.batch_size` loop and slices of size `self.batch_size`.
- With `run/preprocess_sentence.sh` and `batch_size=1`, sentence caches should now be materialized one sentence chunk at a time instead of one full document's sentence set at a time.

## What was verified
- Verified that `python -m py_compile src/materialize/materialize.py src/preprocess.py` succeeds after the batch-flush fix.
- Confirmed by code inspection that the earlier warning lines such as `sentence token count exceeded document token count` come from the approximate sentence-token offset bookkeeping in `_split_document_into_sentences()` and are separate from the OOM cause.

## Open issues
- The sentence token-count warning still exists. It reflects that sentence spans are reconstructed by re-encoding each sentence independently, so `chunk_starts` / `chunk_ends` remain approximate under `segment_unit=sentence`.
- The full `run/preprocess_sentence.sh` job has not yet been rerun to completion after the batch-flush fix, so runtime and memory behavior still need an end-to-end confirmation.

## Next steps
- Rerun `./run/preprocess_sentence.sh` and confirm that materialization proceeds past the previous OOM point.
- If memory pressure remains, inspect whether cache tensors should be freed more aggressively after each batch, but do not change the materialization logic further unless the rerun still fails.

# 2026-04-13

## Objective of the session
- Estimate how much adaptive boundary repair would cost, in tokens, under the current sentence-level `compare` setup.

## What was changed
- Ran a local cost-analysis script on the current post-`compare` selected sentence set.
- Estimated repair overhead for boundary windows of `16`, `32`, and `64` tokens.
- Reported two cost views:
  - `naive`: sum of left/right repair tokens for every boundary, allowing repeated recomputation
  - `unique-touched`: upper bound assuming overlapping repair regions are fused so each selected token is recomputed at most once

## What was verified
- Current post-selection token budget across the first `20` queries is `61390` tokens.
- Estimated global repair overhead ratios:
  - window `16`: naive `0.762`, unique-touched `0.670`
  - window `32`: naive `1.339`, unique-touched `0.907`
  - window `64`: naive `1.803`, unique-touched `0.984`
- Per-query `32`-token repair windows are also expensive:
  - average naive ratio `1.353`
  - average unique-touched ratio `0.910`
- This suggests sentence-level adaptive repair can easily consume most or all of the selected cache budget unless repair is applied very selectively.

## Open issues
- These estimates assume every boundary is repaired; a boundary-scoring policy might reduce the cost materially if only a small subset of boundaries are repaired.
- The analysis is still a token-budget estimate, not a measured latency benchmark.

## Next steps
- Estimate break-even costs for repairing only the top `x%` of boundaries by a future boundary score.
- Compare those estimated budgets against actual `cache_on` accuracy recovery once a selective repair prototype exists.

# 2026-04-13

## Objective of the session
- Fix the repeated `rope_scaling.original_max_position_embeddings` warning during cache shifting.

## What was changed
- Updated `src/cache_utils.py` in `_shift_rotary_keys()`.
- Previously the helper rebuilt `LlamaRotaryEmbedding` with:
  - `max_position_embeddings = max(position_offset + 1, 8192)`
- This could recreate a config where:
  - `original_max_position_embeddings = 8192`
  - `max_position_embeddings = 8192`
- That equality triggers the repeated warning from the transformers RoPE validation path.
- The logic now uses:
  - `max_position_embeddings = max(position_offset + seq_len, original_max_position_embeddings + 1)`
- This keeps the configured RoPE context strictly larger than `original_max_position_embeddings` and also accounts for the full shifted sequence length rather than only the first shifted token.

## What was verified
- Confirmed that `src/cache_utils.py` compiles with `python -m py_compile`.
- Confirmed by code inspection that the updated formula avoids the `8192 == 8192` warning condition.

## Open issues

- Per-step `attention_mask` allocation is still present and may remain a secondary bottleneck after grouping removal.

## Next steps

  - `decode per batch` drops materially

# 2026-05-01

## Objective of the session
- Record the current reasoning about why subchunk cache load remains slower than MatKV and what storage-layout direction now looks most promising before making another implementation change.

## What was changed
- No source-code changes were made under `src/`, `run/`, or `test/` in this session update.
- Reviewed the latest cache-load profiling results and the implications of several candidate ideas:
  - per-sentence/per-subchunk baseline load
  - document-local synthetic shard replay
  - `~256`-token sentence-boundary parent-window shard replay
  - model quantization vs KV quantization as possible ways to strengthen subchunk throughput claims
- Recorded the current interpretation:
  - the dominant remaining subchunk disadvantage is still cache load
  - the main cause appears to be many sparse per-subchunk file loads rather than prefill/decode overhead
  - naive grouping by document or by document-order `256`-token windows did not help because selected sentences are too sparse relative to those storage units
  - the failed `256`-window replay indicates a retrieval/storage alignment problem, not simply “load unit too small”
- Recorded the emerging storage idea that seems most compatible with the research goals:
  - keep fine-grained sentence/subchunk selection for accuracy
  - avoid DRAM-caching-centric claims as the main research message
  - instead test a storage redesign such as:
    - document-local flat binary KV blobs
    - a global or document-level index mapping `chunk_id -> file, offset, length, shape, dtype`
    - partial reads of only the required byte ranges
    - optional range coalescing for nearby offsets inside the same document blob
- Recorded the current reasoning about quantization:
  - model quantization is a common optimization that likely weakens subchunk-vs-MatKV system-latency claims because it reduces compute, where subchunk already had an advantage
  - KV quantization is more directly relevant to cache-serving overhead and could help subchunk more, but it also carries higher accuracy-drop risk

## What was verified
- Verified from the latest synthetic parent-window shard replay that:
  - shard coverage was complete after the mapping bug fix
  - `torch.load` call count dropped only modestly relative to baseline
  - `torch.load` time increased drastically because each loaded shard contained many sentences that were not actually needed
- Verified from discussion of the storage/retrieval mismatch that:
  - matching MatKV’s nominal `256`-token load unit is not sufficient by itself
  - what matters is whether the selected evidence actually uses most of the loaded unit
  - subchunk accuracy may be benefiting precisely from this sparse fine-grained selection, even while that same sparsity hurts cache-load efficiency
- After reviewing the synthetic parent-window replay code, identified an important limitation in the earlier interpretation:
  - parent-window shards were built in document-offset order
  - but runtime replay was still loading them in the original selected chunk order rather than a `(parent_doc_id, offset)`-sorted order
  - this means the earlier replay was a valid stress test for the naive read order, but not a fair test of locality-aware shard loading
- Updated the test-only shard replay profiler to add a second parent-window variant that:
  - preloads the request’s required shards in `(parent_doc_id, shard_start, shard_end)` order
  - then assembles the request back in its original selected chunk order
  - reports this sorted-load variant alongside:
    - baseline per-subchunk load
    - naive parent-window shard load

## Open issues
- There is still no reduced-overhead cache format in the codebase that avoids heavy per-file `torch.load` deserialization while preserving fine-grained subchunk selection.
- The current synthetic shard profilers still use `torch.save` / `torch.load`, so they do not yet test the more promising “flat binary + index + partial read” direction.
- The corrected sorted-load parent-window replay still needs to be rerun before the `256`-token shard idea is judged more definitively.
- The previous MatKV cache-on vs no-cache comparison was also confounded by prompt serialization mismatch:
  - cache-on reuses raw chunk KV and only appends the query prompt at runtime
  - the old no-cache path inserted explicit passage separators (`\\n\\n`) between chunk texts
  - updated the no-cache prompt builder to concatenate chunk texts without added separators so it is closer to the cache-on serialization
- The MatKV no-cache path also showed a strong batch-size sensitivity bug:
  - `bsz=1` no-cache accuracy was much higher than `bsz>1` under otherwise similar prompt statistics
  - the likely cause was batched decoder-only generation with right padding on full prompts
  - updated `LLMModel._tokenize_full_prompts()` to left-pad full prompts while keeping left-side truncation
- No direct measurement has yet been made for:
  - document-local flat-binary partial reads
  - range-coalesced reads for nearby selected subchunks
  - whether such a layout can bring subchunk cache-load time close enough to MatKV for the current batch-size goal

## Next steps
- Prototype a test-only storage path that writes:
  - document-local KV blobs
  - an index mapping selected subchunk ids to byte offsets and tensor metadata
- Add a profiler that replays current subchunk requests using:
  - the existing per-subchunk `.pt` path
  - the new flat-binary partial-read path
- Compare at minimum:
  - `cache total avg per batch`
  - `torch.load` replacement read time
  - open/read call counts
  - useful loaded bytes vs total loaded bytes
- Only after clarifying that storage-layout effect, revisit:
  - KV quantization
  - cache-load / GPU-transfer pipelining
  - matched end-to-end MatKV vs subchunk throughput claims at `bsz=24` vs `bsz=32`

# 2026-05-01

## Objective of the session
- Record the latest interpretation of the MatKV/subchunk comparison, the cache-load profiling outcomes, and the current research direction before the next implementation change.

## What was changed
- Updated `src/model.py` and `src/infer.py` earlier in the session to make the no-cache prompt path closer to cache-on behavior:
  - removed added passage separators from the no-cache prompt builder by introducing a cache-aligned prompt path
  - changed full-prompt batching for no-cache generation to left padding to avoid the `bsz>1` decoder-only generation failure mode
- Updated `test/profile_cache_load_doc_shard_replay.py` earlier in the session to:
  - fix parent-window shard coverage reconstruction from the sentence DB
  - add a locality-aware `parent_chunk_shard_sorted_load` replay variant
- Updated `docs/handoff.md` throughout the session with those bug fixes and profiling caveats.
- Reviewed the latest experimental outcomes and recorded the current interpretation:
  - `subchunk` still beats `matkv_256` on both F1 and request throughput in the current max-batch-size setup
  - `matkv_1024` can beat the current `subchunk cache-on` F1, but this should be treated as a trade-off reference rather than the main baseline
  - `subchunk no-cache` F1 (`0.4367`) being much higher than `subchunk cache-on` F1 (`0.3957`) suggests the remaining quality gap is largely in cache reuse / assembly fidelity rather than retrieval potential
  - the synthetic `256`-token parent-window shard idea is still not promising even after load-order sorting:
    - sorting shard loads by `(parent_doc_id, shard_start, shard_end)` helped substantially
    - but the replay remained much slower than baseline
    - this points to overfetch plus `torch.load`/deserialization cost as the main issue, not just bad read order
  - current evidence suggests:
    - sparse fine-grained selection may be one reason subchunk can outperform small MatKV baselines on accuracy
    - but that same sparsity makes naive chunk grouping ineffective for cache loading
  - model quantization is likely a weak or even unfavorable way to strengthen subchunk-vs-MatKV system claims because it reduces compute, where subchunk already had an advantage
  - KV quantization is more directly relevant to cache-serving overhead and could help subchunk more, but it carries higher accuracy-drop risk
  - the most promising next systems direction is no longer naive shard grouping, but:
    - document-local flat binary KV blobs
    - explicit index metadata (`chunk_id -> file, offset, length, shape, dtype`)
    - partial reads of only required byte ranges
    - optional range coalescing for nearby subchunks in the same document
- Computed current per-document total cache-length distributions for the populated datasets:
  - `subchunk_sent`:
    - docs: `1722`
    - mean: `1465.42`
    - median: `716.50`
    - p90: `3608.50`
    - p95: `5412.35`
    - max: `14092`
  - `matkv_1024`:
    - docs: `1722`
    - mean: `1478.74`
    - median: `731.50`
    - p90: `3613.70`
    - p95: `5462.20`
    - max: `14136`
  - Interpretation:
    - total per-document cache length is nearly the same between the two
    - the real difference is not document total length, but how many cache pieces each document is split into and how those pieces are accessed at runtime

## What was verified
- Verified that the earlier `matkv_1024` no-cache result with very low score was partly confounded by batching behavior:
  - `bsz=1` no-cache F1 was much higher than `bsz>1`
  - this strongly indicated a batched no-cache generation bug rather than a pure retrieval/context problem

  - no-cache had been disadvantaged by explicit text separators and right-padding batch tokenization

- This final profiler does not modify `src/eval.py` or `src/infer.py`.
- Instead, it wraps `LLMModel.generate_response()` only inside the test script:
  - `prefill_microbatch_size=full` uses the normal eval-path `generate_response()`
  - `prefill_microbatch_size=4/5/...` keeps the real eval decode path but splits only the cache-on prefill forward into microbatches, merges the per-microbatch `past_key_values`, and then calls the existing no-trim decode path
- The profiler reports per-batch:

  - `prefill`
  - `decode`
  - `total`
  - and final throughput

## Open issues
- The token-level probe removes the earlier unit-size confound for concentration metrics, but it is still only a layer-0 analysis.
- Top-32 and top-128 token masses are not directly comparable across MatKV and subchunk as absolute concentration indicators because the total cache lengths differ greatly; the most reliable cross-method concentration metrics are:
  - top-1% token mass
  - top-5% token mass
  - normalized token entropy
  - token-level Gini
- The resulting pattern is mixed:
  - MatKV shows higher top-1% / top-5% mass and higher Gini, which indicates stronger concentration on a small subset of cache tokens.
  - But normalized token entropy is nearly the same between MatKV and subchunk at layer 0.
- Therefore the token-level evidence supports a narrower claim than the earlier unit-level story:
  - MatKV attention is more sharply concentrated on a small set of cache tokens.
  - subchunk attention is less peak-concentrated over cache tokens and places more mass on query-side tokens.
  - This is consistent with, but does not yet prove, the hypothesis that subchunk is less vulnerable to a single coarse cached representation being distorted by PIC.

## Next steps
- If mechanism analysis continues, prefer token-level or answer-support-span-level probes over unit-level concentration metrics.
- A stronger follow-up would compare attention concentration or hidden-state drift on answer-supporting tokens/spans rather than over all cached tokens.

  - subchunk has larger **raw** sink mass because it has many more boundaries
  - but MatKV has far larger **sink enrichment**, especially from layer 2 onward and in late layers
- This is the clearest mechanistic signal observed so far and is consistent with the EPIC-style sink hypothesis.

## Next steps
- Use sink enrichment, not raw sink share, as the main analysis variable when comparing units with different boundary counts.
- If needed, add a no-cache counterpart later to measure explicit sink-delta, but the current cache-on statistics already suggest that coarse MatKV units suffer much stronger sink amplification than subchunk units.

  - cache-off: `EM 0.595 / F1 0.7259`

    - cache-off `EM 0.65 / F1 0.7466`

    - cache-off EM in `11` cases
    - cache-off F1 in `16` cases

    - on-only `47`
    - off-only `20`
    - both `99`
    - neither `34`
- In both methods, cache-off outputs are noticeably longer and more likely to contain tails such as:
  - repeated answer phrases
  - `Passage:` / `Question:` leakage
  - `Note:` / `Source:` continuations
  - answer plus explanatory continuation

## Open issues
- The cache-off drop is not purely a scoring artifact:
  - cleaner recovers a meaningful subset of failures
  - but cache-on still wins many more samples even before cleaning
- Both methods can still produce prompt leakage or instruction-copy artifacts in some cache-on outputs, though it is more common/severe in cache-off.
- The current conclusion is specific to the present prompt / generation setup for `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` and should not yet be generalized beyond this setup.

### Threshold + Windowed Score on the same mini100 subsets

#### Method note
- Added a test-only `Threshold + Windowed Score` variant to `test/eval_globaltopn_vs_window.py`.
- This family:
  - computes sentence relevance scores
  - keeps sentences whose score is above a relative cutoff within the query-local score range
  - adds a small bonus to `±1` neighbor sentences of the kept centers
  - re-applies the same cutoff after score shaping
  - preserves original sentence order within each document
- Swept only three threshold values:
  - `0.3`
  - `0.4`
  - `0.5`
- Kept `window_score_bonus_ratio = 0.2` fixed in this first pass.

#### Path correction
- `HotpotQA mini100` and `2Wiki mini100` valid subset assets were found under:

- Earlier valid mini100 results remain trustworthy because the non-zero selection statistics and successful cache loads match the `_nvme` assets; only one aborted intermediate rerun that accidentally pointed to the empty stub DB should be discarded.

### 2Wiki mini100: Threshold + Windowed Score bonus sweep at fixed `thr50`

#### Objective
- Test the user hypothesis that `2Wiki` might benefit from a stronger local-context bonus because:
  - sentence-only is weak
  - `Local Expansion` helps over sentence-only
  - `Threshold + Windowed Score` already beats `MatKV-1024` on cache-on
- Keep threshold fixed at the current best cache-on value:
  - `thr50`
- Sweep only the neighbor bonus:
  - `0.2` (existing baseline)
  - `0.4`
  - `0.6`
  - `0.8`

#### Results
- cache-off
  - `bonus 0.2`: `F1 0.2534`, `1069.61` tokens/query
  - `bonus 0.4`: `F1 0.2624`, `1072.16` tokens/query
  - `bonus 0.6`: `F1 0.2902`, `1058.03` tokens/query
  - `bonus 0.8`: `F1 0.2885`, `1055.12` tokens/query
- cache-on
  - `bonus 0.2`: `F1 0.3151`, `1069.61` tokens/query
  - `bonus 0.4`: `F1 0.3067`, `1072.16` tokens/query
  - `bonus 0.6`: `F1 0.3131`, `1058.03` tokens/query
  - `bonus 0.8`: `F1 0.3131`, `1055.12` tokens/query

#### Interpretation
- Increasing the local bonus did **not** improve the best `cache-on` result.
- The original lower-bonus setting remained best on the real target metric:
  - `cache-on bonus 0.2 = 0.3151`
- A larger bonus did help `cache-off` somewhat:
  - best was `bonus 0.6 = 0.2902`
- But that improvement did **not** transfer to cache-on.
- Therefore the simple story
  - “2Wiki needs more local context, so just raise the neighbor bonus”
  does **not** hold under the current cache-on protocol.
- This weakens the idea that the remaining gap is mainly caused by underweighting adjacent sentences during selection.
- It instead suggests that:
  - either the current score-shaping mechanism is not the right way to inject local information
  - or the relevant local information for 2Wiki is not captured just by giving stronger weight to adjacent sentences at selection time
  - or the cache-on path needs a different kind of context-aware materialization rather than a stronger selection-time bonus

### Cache-off serialization artifact check: document-grouped sentence assembly

#### Change
- Updated `test/eval_globaltopn_vs_window.py` cache-off prompt assembly only.
- Old behavior:
  - every selected sentence was serialized as its own passage
  - so `\n\n` appeared between all selected sentences, even within one document
- New test-only behavior:
  - selected sentences are still chosen the same way
  - but selected sentences from the same document are concatenated into one passage
  - `\n\n` is inserted only between documents
- Cache-on was unchanged.

  - `2Wiki` also no longer shows a strong cache-off advantage for `Local Expansion`; `threshold_windowed_thr30/40` are now slightly better than sentence-only and fixed local expansion.
- Therefore the earlier statement
  - “cache-off 기준으로 local expansion은 TriviaQA를 제외하면 대체로 우세했다”

## Additional verification
- To isolate whether the earlier adaptive drop was just a threshold issue or a broader cache-on issue, reran the full subchunk family on the same `mini100` subsets:
  - `sentence_topn12`
  - `fixed_pm1_topn12`
  - `adaptive_docshare40_topn12_else_topn24`
  - each under both `cache-off` and `cache-on`

### Subchunk-family cache-off/on on the same mini100 subsets

#### TriviaQA mini100
- cache-off
  - `sentence_topn12`: `F1 0.7457`, `469.49` tokens/query
  - `fixed_pm1_topn12`: `F1 0.7604`, `894.85` tokens/query
  - `adaptive(0.4)`: `F1 0.8041`, `1532.23` tokens/query
- cache-on
  - `sentence_topn12`: `F1 0.7942`, `469.59` tokens/query
  - `fixed_pm1_topn12`: `F1 0.8232`, `894.90` tokens/query
  - `adaptive(0.4)`: `F1 0.7701`, `1532.09` tokens/query
- interpretation
  - `sentence` and `fixed` both improved under cache-on.
  - only `adaptive` degraded.
  - this means the earlier TriviaQA issue is not a generic subchunk cache-on weakness; it is specific to the adaptive policy.

#### HotpotQA mini100
- cache-off
  - `sentence_topn12`: `F1 0.3782`, `581.23` tokens/query
  - `fixed_pm1_topn12`: `F1 0.4175`, `1094.42` tokens/query
  - `adaptive(0.4)`: `F1 0.4153`, `1243.36` tokens/query
- cache-on
  - `sentence_topn12`: `F1 0.4064`, `581.23` tokens/query
  - `fixed_pm1_topn12`: `F1 0.3678`, `1094.42` tokens/query
  - `adaptive(0.4)`: `F1 0.3139`, `1243.36` tokens/query
- interpretation
  - `sentence` improved under cache-on.
  - both `fixed` and `adaptive` degraded, and the larger-context adaptive policy degraded the most.
  - this suggests the HotpotQA cache-on problem is not just the adaptive threshold; the local-window-expansion style policies are the unstable part.

#### 2Wiki mini100
- cache-off
  - `sentence_topn12`: `F1 0.2946`, `597.91` tokens/query
  - `fixed_pm1_topn12`: `F1 0.3102`, `1018.55` tokens/query
  - `adaptive(0.4)`: `F1 0.3262`, `1277.77` tokens/query
- cache-on
  - `sentence_topn12`: `F1 0.2265`, `597.91` tokens/query
  - `fixed_pm1_topn12`: `F1 0.2790`, `1018.55` tokens/query
  - `adaptive(0.4)`: `F1 0.2716`, `1277.77` tokens/query
- interpretation
  - all three subchunk policies degraded under cache-on.
  - the degradation is largest for `sentence_topn12`, smaller for `fixed`, and moderate for `adaptive`.
  - this suggests a broader 2Wiki cache-on issue rather than a threshold-only problem.

### Takeaway
- The cache-on degradation is not uniform across datasets or policies.
- `TriviaQA`: only the adaptive policy gets worse.
- `HotpotQA`: `sentence` gets better, but `fixed` and `adaptive` get worse.
- `2Wiki`: all subchunk policies get worse.
- Therefore, the earlier discrepancy cannot be explained solely by “0.4 was chosen on cache-off”.
- The stronger hypothesis is that cache-on interacts with context shape / selection policy differently by dataset, and adaptive threshold choice is only part of the story.

## Objective of the session
- Test whether the cache-off serializer variants can be approximated at cache-on time by trimming the trailing `"\n\n"` sentence suffix from precomputed sentence caches.

## Main takeaways
- `1번` remains the strongest cache-on serializer overall.
- `2번` (`adjacent_runs`) underperforms `1번` on all three datasets for the targeted variants.
- `3번` (`adjacent_runs_no_doc_boundary`) is even worse overall; removing the document boundary at cache-on time is strongly harmful.
- Therefore:
  - the cache-off serializer gains do **not** transfer to cache-on by simple runtime suffix trimming
  - serializer-only cache-on manipulation is not enough
  - the remaining promising direction is representation/materialization change rather than boundary trimming alone

## Open issues
- Cache-off and cache-on now show a clear mismatch:
  - some cache-off serializers are strong
  - but suffix-trimmed cache-on analogues are weaker
- This suggests the bottleneck is likely not string serialization alone, but the sentence-level cache representation itself.

## Next steps
- Treat serializer-only cache-on trimming as largely negative evidence.
- If continuing on the cache representation side, prefer:
  - left-context-aware sentence KV
  - span-aware materialization
  - or doc-start-aware dual cache variants
- Separate next direction already discussed:
  - inspect Provence-selected sentence outputs
  - distill lightweight selection signals from Provence as a teacher.

## 2026-05-19 (space-prefix sentence cache experiment)

### Objective
- Test a new sentence cache format intended to better approximate `cache-off 3-B` during `cache-on`.
- The new cache unit format is:
  - `[space_token] + tokenize(sentence) + [newline2_token]`
  - where:
    - `" "` token id = `220`
    - `"\n\n"` token id = `271`
- Restrict the rerun to:
  - `mini100`
  - `cache-on`
  - `3-B = adjacent_runs_no_doc_boundary`
  - subchunk methods only (no MatKV rerun)

### What was changed
- Updated `src/materialize/materialize.py`:
  - added `sentence_cache_token_format`
  - supported values:
    - `legacy`
    - `space_prefix_newline_suffix`
  - for the new format, sentence visible tokens are built as:
    - `[220] + sentence_token_ids + [271]`
- Updated `src/preprocess.py`:
  - threaded `sentence_cache_token_format` into `DocumentPreprocessor`
- Updated `test/eval_globaltopn_vs_window.py`:
  - added `cacheon_cache_token_format`
  - generalized cache trimming to allow both prefix and suffix trimming
  - implemented `3-B`-aware prefix/suffix keep masks for the new cache format
  - added `avg_cached_tokens_per_query` recording for cache-on runs

### What was verified
- Tokenizer checks for `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`:
  - `" "` -> single token `220`
  - `"  "` -> single token `256`
  - `"\n\n"` -> single token `271`
- Also verified:
  - leading-space forms like `" Hello"` / `" Adam"` are typically merged into a single token
  - therefore a plain string-level prefix space is **not** trim-safe
  - this motivated the explicit `[220] + sentence + [271]` design

- New sentence caches were materialized successfully for all three mini100 datasets:
  - `longbench-triviaqa-mini100-sent-seed42/sent_spaceprefix`
  - `longbench-hotpotqa-mini100-sent-seed42/sent_spaceprefix`
  - `longbench-2wiki-mini100-sent-seed42/sent_spaceprefix`

- `TriviaQA mini100`, `cache-on`, `3-B` was evaluated with the new cache format.
- Result: severe degradation across all tested variants.

### Open issues
- The new cache format causes severe `TriviaQA cache-on` degradation, much worse than the earlier sentence-cache variants.
- Current evidence suggests:
  - `3-B` runtime assembly is not the main failure point
  - the explicit independent prefix-space token design may itself be too unnatural for the model
- Because `cache-off 3-B` joins contiguous runs with a normal textual space, but the new cache uses:
  - independent prefix space token
  - sentence tokens without the usual merged leading-space form
  this may distort the model's expected prefix distribution.
- `HotpotQA` and `2Wiki` were **not** rerun yet under this new format.

### Next steps
- Do **not** assume the poor results invalidate `3-B` itself; they currently invalidate this specific cache encoding.
- If continuing on separator-aware cache design:
  - reconsider whether explicit independent prefix-space tokens are acceptable
  - or move to a different representation-oriented direction
- The strongest alternative already discussed is still:
  - left-context-aware sentence KV
  - e.g. materialize from `sent_{i-1} + " " + sent_i + "\n\n"`
  - store only the `sent_i` segment KV

    - `F1 = 0.2990`
  - delta:

  - `cache-on elapsed = 31.66s`
  - `avg_cached_tokens_per_query = 1184.6`

### Open issues
- This was only a tiny sanity slice:
  - one dataset
  - one method family (`fixed_pm1_topn12`)
  - ten examples
- The improvement is promising but too small to draw a general conclusion.
- The current script only tests the `reuse curr after prev+curr` construction.

- If this direction is worth continuing, scale the same script gradually:

  - `pair_curr_token_ids`

## 2026-05-20 (ROPE shift correctness check)

### Objective
- Check whether the current runtime ROPE cache-shift logic itself is wrong in the
  `run/preprocess_matkv.sh` / `cache-on` path.

### What was changed
- No source code change for this check.
- Ran an isolated synthetic test on the current `src/cache_utils.py`
  `shift_rotary_cache()` implementation.

### What was verified
- The current implementation applies a **constant offset rotation** to an
  already locally-rotated cache.
- This is mathematically the correct transformation for converting local
  positions `p` into global positions `p + offset`.
- Synthetic random-key check:
  - compare:
    - local rotation at positions `0..L-1`, then current `shift_rotary_cache(offset)`
    - direct absolute rotation at positions `offset..offset+L-1`
  - result:
    - mean abs diff: `5.33e-08`
    - max abs diff: `1.70e-06`
    - `allclose(atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4) = True`

### Open issues
- End-to-end quality gaps are therefore unlikely to come from the rotary
  shift formula itself.
- Remaining mismatch is more likely due to:
  - independently materialized chunk/subchunk caches
  - prompt/query serialization differences
  - cache assembly assumptions

### Next steps
- Treat the current rotary shift implementation as mathematically correct.
- Focus debugging on cache assembly / chunk independence / prompt alignment
  rather than on the ROPE shift formula itself.

## 2026-05-22 (HotpotQA 20-doc fastcoref vs attention semantic-chunking probe)

### Objective
- Implement a second semantic-chunking probe that uses last-layer attention between adjacent sentences as the merge signal, then compare it against the current fastcoref-based heuristic on a small HotpotQA sample.

### What was changed
- Added:
  - `test/probe_semantic_chunking_attention_compare.py`
- The new probe keeps the existing `blingfire` sentence splitter and compares:
  - `fastcoref_heuristic`
  - `last_layer_attention_backward_dependency`
- Attention scoring policy:
  - prefill `s_i + "\n\n" + s_{i+1}`
  - read the final layer self-attention
  - compute the average backward attention mass from `s_{i+1}` tokens to `s_i` tokens
  - choose a per-document threshold that matches the fastcoref merge-count on that document
- Also tightened probe stability:
  - changed the attention probe default `attention_batch_size` from `16` to `1` to avoid OOM from long sentence pairs
  - reused a single `fastcoref` model instance across documents instead of reinitializing it per document
  - clamped out-of-range fastcoref mention spans before converting clusters into sentence-boundary links
- Updated:
  - `test/probe_semantic_chunking_fastcoref.py`
  with the same reusable-model and span-clamping stability fixes.

### What was verified
- `python -m py_compile` passed for:
  - `test/probe_semantic_chunking_attention_compare.py`
  - `test/probe_semantic_chunking_fastcoref.py`
- Ran the new probe on:
  - `HotpotQA`
  - `20` sampled documents
  - `seed=42`
- Generated outputs:
  - `outputs/semantic_chunking/hotpotqa_fastcoref_probe_20docs.json`
  - `outputs/semantic_chunking/hotpotqa_attention_probe_20docs.json`
  - `outputs/semantic_chunking/hotpotqa_fastcoref_vs_attention_compare_20docs.json`
- Aggregate length comparison:
  - sentence baseline:
    - count `897`
    - mean `34.84`
    - median `27`
    - p95 `77`
    - max `1037`
  - fastcoref chunks:
    - count `538`
    - mean `58.03`
    - median `39`
    - p95 `126`
    - max `1056`
  - attention chunks:
    - count `559`
    - mean `55.84`
    - median `42`
    - p95 `122`
    - max `1056`
- Sentence-count-per-chunk distributions:
  - fastcoref:
    - `1:316, 2:132, 3:58, 4:19, 5:11, 6:2`
  - attention:
    - `1:339, 2:139, 3:56, 4:17, 5:5, 6:2, 7:1`
- Boundary-level comparison:
  - total differing boundaries across 20 docs: `207`
  - average differing boundaries per doc: `10.35`
- Representative pattern from `doc_1043.txt`:
  - fastcoref merges explicit referential continuations like
    - `Mimosa aculeaticarpa ...`
    - `It is commonly known ...`
  - but attention sometimes refuses those merges when the backward attention score falls below the per-doc threshold
  - attention also creates some merges with no fastcoref signal, e.g. descriptive continuation pairs like
    - `The alternate leaves are bi-pinnate ...`
    - `The flowers are white or pale pink ...`

### Open issues
- The attention policy is not simply a stricter version of fastcoref:
  - it suppresses some pronoun/coref merges
  - but also adds new topical-description merges with no coref signal
- Because the threshold is chosen to match the fastcoref merge count per document, the comparison is controlled for merge budget but not yet tuned for quality.
- Extremely long single-sentence artifacts from upstream `blingfire` splitting still propagate into both probes, which is why max chunk length remains very large (`1056`).

### Next steps
- Inspect whether the added attention-only merges are semantically desirable or just topic-cohesion noise.
- Decide whether the attention score should be combined with a referential signal instead of replacing it outright.
- If this line continues, consider:
  - requiring an explicit pronoun/coref cue for merge, then using attention only as a reranker
  - or adding a hard cap to every final chunk, including 1- and 2-sentence chunks.

    - p95 `125.0`
  - `0.72`
    - chunk count `616`
    - merge count `281`
    - blocked by cap `53`
    - mean chunk length `50.69`
    - p95 `115.5`
  - `0.73`
    - chunk count `729`
    - merge count `168`
    - blocked by cap `23`
    - mean chunk length `42.85`
    - p95 `87.2`
  - `0.75`
    - chunk count `869`
    - merge count `28`
    - blocked by cap `2`
    - mean chunk length `35.96`
    - p95 `77.0`
- Interpretation from morphology alone:
  - `0.68~0.70` is too aggressive
  - `0.74~0.76` is too conservative and nearly collapses back to sentence-level units
  - `0.71~0.72` looks like the most plausible compromise range before downstream QA evaluation

### Open issues
- This sweep only tunes morphology:
  - chunk count
  - merge count
  - token-length distribution
- It does not yet tell us which threshold is best for retrieval/materialization quality downstream.
- Very long single-sentence artifacts from the upstream splitter still remain possible and can dominate the tail even under attention-based merging.

### Next steps
- Use `0.71` and `0.72` as first candidates for downstream semantic-subchunk retrieval/materialization experiments.
- If needed, compare:
  - attention-only
  - fastcoref-only
  - attention gated by referential cues
  under the same 128-token cap.
